data.title: A quiet place to stay a while.
data.intro: SageHaven is a small group of houses in the hills, run as places to be quiet in. This page is about the places and how we use them.

children.text: SageHaven began with an empty timber lodge on a lake and a question: what would people do with a few days and no obligations? We lent the lodge to friends for a weekend, put out cushions and rang a bell in the morning. Most of what we do now comes from what worked that weekend.
The places

We run retreats in four houses: Larkmere Lodge on the lake, Highfold Cabins on a ridge, Pinewhistle Hall in the woods and Gullcove House by the sea. Each is old, plain and warm. None has a television.
How we think about it

Meditation here means sitting still, walking slowly and paying attention. We teach it simply and we do not ask anyone to adopt a belief. Teachers are available during the day for questions, and every instruction is optional.
What we do not do
We do not make claims about health. We do not sell supplements or run seminars.
Visiting
Browse the upcoming retreats and send an enquiry. We reply within two working days with availability, rooms and travel details.

data.title: Guest guidelines
data.intro: A few simple agreements that keep the house quiet for everyone.

children.text: Silence
From the evening bell until after breakfast we ask for silence. On silent days it runs until supper. Notes are fine if something is urgent.
Phones
Phones go in the lockable box on arrival. A landline in the hall is available at any time.
Food
Meals are vegetarian. Tell us about allergies and dietary needs on the enquiry form. We cannot cook separate menus for preference alone.
Leaving early
You can leave at any time. Tell a teacher so we know you are safe and can arrange the transfer.

children.text: What the weekend is like
We arrive on Friday afternoon, settle into our rooms and meet over tea. From Saturday morning the day follows a steady rhythm of short sits, walking, meals and rest.
Instructions are given in plain words and repeated. You can sit on a cushion, a stool or a chair. Nobody is expected to hold a posture.
Who it suits
People who are new to meditation, or who have tried apps at home and want to practise with others in a quiet place. Groups are small, so there is time to ask questions.

children.text: The setting
Larkmere Lodge sits above a quiet bay with a timber deck facing east. Most sits happen there, weather allowing. When it rains we move inside to the long room with the stove.
The two days
Saturday starts at 6:30 with a short sit before breakfast. Between sessions there is time to walk the shore path, read or sleep. Sunday finishes with lunch at 1 pm.

children.text: Days in the woods
The middle day is held in silence from waking until supper. The other days are lighter: guided sits in the morning and evening, and time to walk the marked trails in between.
Rooms and food
Rooms are plain and warm, with wool blankets and a window onto the trees. Meals are vegetarian and cooked in the house kitchen. Tell us about allergies when you enquire.

children.text: A full week
Highfold Cabins stand on a ridge with a view down the valley. Each day follows the same shape, so there is little to decide: sit, walk, eat, rest, sit again.
The silent day
On day four we keep silence from the morning bell until supper. Teachers are available for a short private word if you need one.
Before you come
You will need walking shoes and warm layers. Mornings on the ridge are cool even in May.

children.text: What we did
A full week of sitting and walking, with a silent day on the fourth day and an afternoon of apple picking in the valley orchard.

data.title: Wake-up bell
data.text: A soft bell, then a short sit before anyone speaks. Tea is waiting in the hall.

data.title: Breakfast in silence
data.text: Porridge, bread, fruit and eggs from the valley. We eat slowly and look out of the window.

data.title: Guided sit and walk
data.text: Thirty minutes sitting, ten minutes walking, repeated. A teacher gives short instructions.

data.title: Lunch and free time
data.text: The long break. Nap, read, swim or walk the trail. No programme until the afternoon.

data.title: Stretching on the deck
data.text: Gentle movement on mats in the afternoon light. Easy to do in your own clothes.

data.title: Evening sit
data.text: The last group practice, then supper and quiet talk by the stove.

data.title: What a silent morning is actually like
data.summary: The first hour without talking feels long. By the third day it feels ordinary. Here is how the mornings run.

children.text: On the first morning at Larkmere Lodge most guests look slightly lost. The bell rings, tea is poured and nobody says anything. People look at their cups a lot.
The first day
You notice noise you had stopped hearing: your own thoughts, cutlery, the stove ticking as it cools. Some people find this uncomfortable. That is normal and it passes.
By the third day
Breakfast takes longer because nobody is rushing. People start to nod at each other across the table. We have never needed more instructions than that.

data.title: Packing for a quiet week
data.summary: A short list of what to bring, and what to leave at home.

children.text: You do not need special clothes. Loose trousers, a few warm layers and a pair of slippers cover most of it.
Bring
Walking shoes, a water bottle, a notebook, a torch for the path at night and any medication you take.
Leave at home
Work laptops, headphones and anything you plan to scroll. We keep a lockable box for phones and most guests are glad to use it. There is a landline in the hall for urgent calls.

data.title: Sitting on a chair is fine
data.summary: You do not need to cross your legs. Cushion, stool or chair: choose what lets you stay still.

children.text: Many first-time guests arrive worried about posture. We keep a row of chairs in every sitting room and nobody comments on who uses them.
What matters
A steady back, hands resting somewhere comfortable and a position you can keep for twenty minutes. That is all we ask.
Try it at home
Pick a chair with a firm seat. Sit forward on the edge, feet flat. Set a timer for ten minutes and watch your breathing.

data.title: Why we keep groups small
data.summary: Fourteen guests is the most we take. The reasons are practical.

children.text: A group of fourteen can eat at two long tables, sit in one room and walk the shore path without crowding.
What a small group changes
Teachers learn everyone's name on day one. Meals stay quiet because nobody is hiding. If someone is struggling, we notice by lunch.
The limit
We have been asked to take larger groups. We prefer to run an extra retreat.
